newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU gets new C.Lyonnais recovery plan.
newsitem.headline: EU gets new C.Lyonnais recovery plan.

text.p: The European Commission said on Friday it had received a revised recovery plan for French state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais, but declined to comment on its substance.
"I can confirm that we received the plan late on Thursday," Commission spokesman Thierry Daman told reporters.

France's new Socialist government said on Thursday it had submitted the much-awaited plan for EU approval, but added it does not aim for the quick privatisation of the bank sought by the previous government.

EU competition chief Karel Van Miert is expected to frown at the absence of a clear commitment on this point as he has made the sale of troubled public companies a key condition for agreeing to their rescue.

Under a 1995 rescue plan approved by the Commission, Credit Lyonnais was expected to be sold off by the year 2000 after being ridden off of its bad assets in an operation which may ultimately cost 170 billion francs ($27.3 billion) to French taxpayers.

"Privatisation is not the focus of the plan. There were promises made in 1995 in a five-year plan. They will be evaluated in due course in the best interests of Credit Lyonnais and its employees and the interests of the state," a French government spokeswoman said.
The new plan consists mainly in waiving the costs of a loan to finance the spinoff of Lyonnais' loss-making assets into a separate holding company.

The French authorities told the Commission at the end of last year that the loan, which was granted below market rates, would cost Lyonnais 3.0 billion francs in 1996, 2.7 billion francs in 1997 and 2.5 billion francs in 1998.

The bank was forced by the Commission to grant the loan of 135 billion francs at favourable terms to bear some of the burden of its reckless expansion in the early 90s which almost result in its collapse.
Without the Commission's approval to neutralise the cost of the loan the bank's performance would be badly hit, wiping out its expected 1.5 billion francs 1997 net profit.

The Commission is expected to forward the plan to consultancy firm Lehman Brothers, which has been advising it on the case, a Commission source said on Thursday. A final EU decision was unlikely before the end of November, he added.
Thanks to the recent recovery in the bank's performance, the French spokeswoman did not expect any recapitalisations in the near future.
The new plan submitted by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn focuses on improving the profitability of the bank and the disposal of Lyonnais' retail banking network outside France.

"This plan, prepared by Credit Lyonnais, aims to ease the way to its recovery by increasing its profitability... The improvement in profitability is a determining factor in enabling changes in the bank," the Finance Ministry said in a statement.
"Credit Lyonnais will largely free itself from its retail banking activity outside France," it said.
